hook: Line up a solid ball, a soup can and a ring of the same mass at the top of a ramp and let go. Most people bet on the heaviest, or call a tie. The answer depends on neither mass nor size, only on shape: how much of each object’s energy goes into spinning instead of moving along.

ideas: Rolling without slipping: vcm = Rω and Δxcm = RΔθ.
Static friction makes a rolling object spin but does no work: mechanical energy is conserved.
Rolling race: v = √(2gh/(1 + I/MR²)). Mass and radius cancel; smaller I/MR² wins (sphere, disk, hoop). A frictionless sliding block beats them all.
Slipping: v<sub>cm</sub> ≠ Rω; kinetic friction dissipates energy and changes v<sub>cm</sub> and ω until they match.

misconception.wrong: A heavier or bigger ball rolls down a ramp faster, and every object rolling from the same height arrives with the same speed √(2gh).
misconception.right: Mass and radius cancel, but shape does not. Each rolling object splits Mgh between moving and spinning, so it arrives slower than √(2gh), and the one with mass nearest its center (smallest I/MR²) arrives first.

summary: An object rolling without slipping has v_cm = Rω, and its kinetic energy is ½Mv² + ½Iω². Static friction makes it spin without doing work, so mechanical energy is conserved: from rest down a height h, v = √(2gh/(1 + I/MR²)), which depends on shape only. When an object slips, v_cm ≠ Rω and kinetic friction dissipates energy until rolling sets in.
